title: Two-Sample Testing for Random Graphswithout Vertex Correspondence

paper.title: Two-Sample Testing for Random Graphs without Vertex Correspondence
paper.abstract: Abstract Two populations of graphs often have to be compared without any correspondence between their vertices, for instance when networks come from different communities, or when a graph generative model is evaluated against held-out graphs. We study how many graphs such an unaligned two-sample test needs, and which graph statistics can detect which differences. For an Erdős–Rényi null and a planted two-block difference that leaves every expected degree unchanged, we show that m ≍ t − 3 m\asymp t^{-3} graphs per group are necessary and sufficient when the per-graph signal-to-noise ratio is t < 1 t<1 . Signed triangle counts attain this rate, and the lower bound holds for every graph size. With aligned vertices m ≍ t − 1 m\asymp t^{-1} graphs suffice, so misalignment costs a factor of order t − 2 t^{-2} . When the triangle signal cancels, the rate becomes t − 4 t^{-4} and 4 4 -cycles are needed. Statistics built from trees have exactly the same expectation under both hypotheses, and tests based on finitely many of them have asymptotically no power. In the graphon limit, this class includes degree distributions and message-passing graph neural network features. For a non-constant null, a generic difference is visible at first order, and a simple motif test attains the aligned order of sample size, suggesting that misalignment is costly mainly for differences that are invisible at low orders. We also give an exactly valid test for one or two graphs per group, at a cost in power. In our simulations, the fitted exponents are close to the predicted ones ( − 3.04 -3.04 against − 3 -3 for unaligned tests and − 1.07 -1.07 against − 1 -1 for aligned ones), and degree-based and random-GNN evaluation metrics stay at their level in a setting where signed triangles need about 65 65 graphs.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A two-sample test for networks decides whether two samples of graphs come from the same distribution. Often the vertices of different graphs do not correspond, as with friendship networks of different schools, protein networks of different species, or molecules. The same is true when a graph generative model is evaluated, since its samples are compared with held-out graphs through degree distributions, clustering coefficients, subgraph counts or random graph-neural-network embeddings ( You et al., 2018 ; O’Bray et al., 2022 ; Thompson et al., 2022 ; Krimmel et al., 2025 ) . Without a correspondence, a test can only use quantities that do not depend on how each graph is labelled. With aligned vertices, the sample complexity of two-sample testing for inhomogeneous random graphs is well understood ( Ghoshdastidar et al., 2020 ; Chatterjee et al., 2023 ) . Without alignment, many tests have been proposed ( Maugis et al., 2020 ; Bravo-Hermsdorff et al., 2023 ; Shao et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2017 ; Sabanayagam et al., 2021 ) , but two basic questions remain open: how many graphs are needed , and which statistics can detect which differences ? In practice, an evaluation metric that is insensitive to a class of failures reports a good model however many samples are drawn. In this paper, we study both questions for graphon models, in which every graph has its own latent vertex positions. Our results suggest that both answers depend on the lowest order at which a difference becomes visible to label-invariant statistics, and this order can be high for differences that are easy to detect with aligned vertices. • Sample complexity ( Theorem 1 ). For an Erdős–Rényi null and a planted two-block difference that preserves every expected degree, with per-graph signal-to-noise ratio t < 1 t<1 , we prove that m ≍ t − 3 m\asymp t^{-3} graphs per group are necessary and sufficient and that signed triangles are optimal, with a lower bound that holds for every graph size. With aligned vertices m ≍ t − 1 m\asymp t^{-1} graphs suffice, so misalignment costs a factor of order t − 2 t^{-2} . When the triangle signal cancels, the rate becomes t − 4 t^{-4} and 4 4 -cycles are needed ( Proposition 1 ). • Tree statistics ( Theorem 2 ). If the null is regular and the difference preserves degrees, every tree density is exactly unchanged, and tests using finitely many tree statistics have asymptotic power equal to their level. Since degree statistics, colour refinement and message-passing graph neural networks are determined by tree densities on graphons ( Grebík and Rocha, 2022 ; Böker, 2023 ; Böker et al., 2023 ) , they cannot detect such differences either. • Order of visibility ( Theorem 3 ). For a non-constant null, a difference is generically visible at first order, and a motif test that does not know the null needs only order 1 / t 1/t graphs, the aligned rate of Theorem 1 . So the factor t − 2 t^{-2} in Theorem 1 reflects first-order invisibility. • Few graphs and experiments. We give an exact permutation test for one graph per group ( Proposition 2 ), and our simulations confirm the predicted exponents. Degree- and GNN-based metrics miss degree-preserving changes both in simulations and on protein graphs, where degree-corrected signed cycles reach power 1 / 2 1/2 with at most six graphs. The second moment behind our lower bound for one graph is due to Mossel et al. (2015) and Banerjee (2018) , Ghoshdastidar et al. (2017) use the same planted partition as a hard instance for one graph per group, and the sharp aligned threshold m ​ t = 1 mt=1 is known for sparse multilayer block models ( Chatterjee et al., 2022 ) . The population bounds, their comparison with alignment, the distributional invariance of tree statistics and the first-order analysis are new.

sections.heading: Unaligned two-sample testing.
sections.text: We observe G 1 , … , G m ∼ P G_{1},\dots,G_{m}\sim P and G 1 ′ , … , G m ′ ∼ Q G_{1}^{\prime},\dots,G_{m}^{\prime}\sim Q , all independent, and test H 0 : P = Q H_{0}:P=Q against H 1 : P ≠ Q H_{1}:P\neq Q . A test ψ \psi maps the 2 ​ m 2m graphs to { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} , and its risk against a pair of hypotheses is the sum of its type I and type II errors. The samples are unaligned : every graph carries its own latent positions, so a vertex label in one graph says nothing about a vertex label in another. For a graphon model this is automatic, because the law of 𝔾 ⁡ ( n , W ) \mathbb{G}(n,W) is invariant under relabelling. Averaging any test over independent uniform relabellings of each graph therefore preserves both of its errors, and we may restrict attention to (possibly randomized) tests that are invariant under relabelling within each graph. Invariant polynomials of bounded degree are exactly linear combinations of subgraph counts ( Carpentier et al., 2025 , Lemma 3.2) . In the aligned version of the problem, all graphs share one vertex labelling and one set of latent positions.

sections.heading: Consequences for invariant learned features.
sections.text: Colour refinement (the 1 1 -dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm) and message-passing graph neural networks cannot distinguish graphons with equal tree homomorphism densities, since on graphons their expressive power is exactly that of tree densities ( Grebík and Rocha, 2022 ; Böker, 2023 ; Böker et al., 2023 ) , and the same holds for degree statistics. Theorem 2 therefore applies to many two-sample statistics in common use, including maximum mean discrepancies between degree distributions, Weisfeiler–Leman subtree kernels ( Shervashidze et al., 2011 ) , and features from randomly initialized or trained message-passing networks ( Thompson et al., 2022 ) . Against a regular null their population targets coincide for every degree-preserving difference, and for finitely many tree statistics Theorem 2 (ii) gives zero asymptotic power at any fixed m m , whereas clustering coefficients, orbit counts and spectra involve cycles and are not affected. One consequence concerns the evaluation of graph generative models ( O’Bray et al., 2022 ; Thompson et al., 2022 ) . Against a regular null, a model that reproduces the degree structure of its training graphs but gets their community or cycle structure wrong cannot be detected by metrics built from degrees or message passing, as Section 7 shows. Weisfeiler–Leman tests of dimension at least two do not share this limitation, since they determine homomorphism counts of all graphs of treewidth two, cycles included ( Dell et al., 2018 ; Morris et al., 2019 ) . The limitation needs both a degree-preserving difference and a regular null. For a planted subgraph on top of 𝔾 ⁡ ( n , p ) \mathbb{G}(n,p) , which always increases degrees, signed star counts are optimal among constant-degree tests ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Under an irregular null, a vertex at position x x has degree Binomial ⁡ ( n − 1 , d W ​ ( x ) ) \mathrm{Binomial}(n-1,d_{W}(x)) under both hypotheses, so the expected degree histogram is the same. Trees with an internal edge acquire a first-order term, equal to ∬ H ⁡ ( x , y ) ​ d W ​ ( x ) ​ d W ​ ( y ) ​ 𝑑 x ​ 𝑑 y \iint H(x,y)\,d_{W}(x)\,d_{W}(y)\,dx\,dy for the path with three edges and non-zero for generic H H , and colour refinement separates the graphons ( Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 5 Non-constant nulls and first-order visibility
sections.text: The t − 3 t^{-3} rate in Theorem 1 comes from a special feature of the Erdős–Rényi null. There every kernel W F , e W_{F,e} in ( 3 ) is constant, so a difference with zero degree function has ⟨ H , W F , e ⟩ = 0 \langle H,W_{F,e}\rangle=0 for every motif, and it cannot be seen before order three. For a non-constant null the first-order term is generically non-zero, and a simple motif test that does not need to know W W already detects the difference. Theorem 3 (First-order visibility) . Let F F be a fixed graph with v v vertices and e ≥ 1 e\geq 1 edges, and let W W be a graphon. Let D D be the difference between the two sample averages of t inj ​ ( F , ⋅ ) t_{\mathrm{inj}}(F,\cdot) . sections.heading: 6 Testing with one to three graphs per group
sections.text: The rates above matter most for small m m , which is where standard calibrations fail. Permuting whole graphs is exact, but for a two-sided statistic its smallest p p -value is 2 / ( 2 ​ m m ) 2/\binom{2m}{m} , which equals 1 1 , 1 / 3 1/3 and 1 / 10 1/10 for m = 1 , 2 , 3 m=1,2,3 . Normal approximations estimate a variance from only 2 ​ m − 2 2m-2 degrees of freedom, and the network jackknife is conservative in expectation ( Lin et al., 2020 ) . However, graphon models have a simple structure that makes exact tests possible with a single graph per group. Proposition 2 (Exact vertex-split permutation test) . Partition [ n ] [n] into fixed blocks V 1 , … , V B V_{1},\dots,V_{B} . If G ∼ 𝔾 ⁡ ( n , W ) G\sim\mathbb{G}(n,W) , the induced subgraphs G ⁡ [ V 1 ] , … , G ⁡ [ V B ] G[V_{1}],\dots,G[V_{B}] are independent, and G ⁡ [ V b ] ∼ 𝔾 ⁡ ( | V b | , W ) G[V_{b}]\sim\mathbb{G}(|V_{b}|,W) . If both samples come from 𝔾 ⁡ ( n , W ) \mathbb{G}(n,W) and the blocks have equal size, the 2 ​ m ​ B 2mB values of any statistic computed on the induced subgraphs are therefore independent and identically distributed. A permutation test over their group labels has level at most α \alpha for every m m and B B , and a two-sided version can reject as soon as ( 2 ​ m ​ B m ​ B ) ≥ 2 / α \binom{2mB}{mB}\geq 2/\alpha , for instance when m = 1 m=1 and B = 4 B=4 . This uses only motifs inside a block. For signed triangles under an Erdős–Rényi null, a block of size n / B n/B has per-graph signal-to-noise ratio t / B t/B , so the squared signal-to-noise ratio of a graph drops from about t 3 / 6 t^{3}/6 to t 3 / ( 6 ​ B 2 ) t^{3}/(6B^{2}) . With m = 1 m=1 and B = 4 B=4 its power in our experiments is only 0.06 for a first-order visible difference and 0.02 under the Erdős–Rényi null ( Table 1 in Section B.3 ), so it mainly guarantees validity. For a mixture of graphons the blocks are only conditionally independent, so the test is not exact.

sections.heading: 7 Experiments
sections.text: Apart from one study of protein graphs, the experiments use simulated graphs, so the ground truth is known. Every number below is read from result files produced by the scripts in the arXiv ancillary files, which use only NumPy and SciPy. For each test we report m ∗ m^{\ast} , the smallest number of graphs per group at which the power reaches 0.5 0.5 at level 0.05 0.05 , interpolated on a geometric grid of m m . Settings, replicate counts and run times are in Appendix B .

sections.text: Figure 1 uses the planted partition with n = 300 n=300 , p = 1 / 2 p=1/2 and t ∈ { 0.3 , … , 0.9 } t\in\{0.3,\dots,0.9\} . The fitted slopes of log ⁡ m ∗ \log m^{\ast} on log ⁡ t \log t are − 3.04 ± 0.03 -3.04\pm 0.03 for signed triangles (theory − 3 -3 ), − 1.07 ± 0.03 -1.07\pm 0.03 for the aligned spectral test (theory − 1 -1 ), − 0.91 ± 0.02 -0.91\pm 0.02 for Q Q , whose signal-to-noise ratio grows like m ⁡ ( m − 1 ) \sqrt{m(m-1)} at small m m , and − 2.13 ± 0.04 -2.13\pm 0.04 and − 1.97 ± 0.02 -1.97\pm 0.02 for the unaligned-to-aligned ratio (theory − 2 -2 ). sections.heading: Graph evaluation metrics.
sections.text: We test descriptors used to evaluate graph generative models ( You et al., 2018 ; O’Bray et al., 2022 ; Thompson et al., 2022 ) , namely the degree histogram, the clustering histogram, six graphlet counts, the Laplacian spectrum and a randomly initialized graph isomorphism network (GIN) ( Xu et al., 2019 ) , each compared by a Gaussian-kernel MMD ( Gretton et al., 2012 ) , together with signed triangles ( Figure 3 ). Against the planted partition, the degree histogram and the random GIN reject at rates between 0.030 and 0.075 for every m m up to 256 256 , at both t = 0.9 t=0.9 and t = 1.5 t=1.5 , so they stay at the level, as Theorem 2 predicts. Both metrics have power 1.00 with m = 16 m=16 against a degree-heterogeneous graphon of the same edge density, where signed triangles have power 0.05. Signed triangles reach power 0.5 0.5 at m = m= 65.5 for t = 0.9 t=0.9 and m = m= 16.2 for t = 1.5 t=1.5 , against 64.2 and 13.9 predicted by the normal approximation with the moments of Theorem 1 (ii). The clustering histogram needs 196.8 and 40.3 graphs, and the graphlet vector needs > 256 >256 because edge-density fluctuations, which move all counts together, dominate its kernel distance. The right panel of Figure 3 models a generator that reproduces degrees exactly but destroys cycle structure, with group 2 consisting of planted-partition graphs with t = 2 t=2 after degree-preserving double-edge swaps. Signed triangles detect the change with m = m= 7.4 graphs, clustering with 19.3 and the spectrum with 61.2, but the degree and GIN metrics never exceed a rejection rate of 0.090.

sections.heading: Irregular nulls and protein graphs.
sections.text: Under two irregular nulls, SMOOTH and a rank-one graphon, the random GIN detects a degree-preserving difference that is correlated with the degree profile, with power 0.80 and 1.00 at m = 64 m=64 , through the first-order term of the 3 3 -edge path ( Section B.5 , where the signal is above the one-graph threshold). It stays at the level, with rejection rates between 0.015 and 0.095 up to m = 256 m=256 (Monte Carlo s.e. 0.015 0.015 ), when the difference is orthogonal to the eigenfunctions of the null, which leaves every path density unchanged ( Proposition 5 ). On protein graphs from two generative-model benchmarks ( Section B.6 ), rewiring 5 % 5\% of the edges of each graph by degree-preserving swaps removes about a quarter of its triangles. The degree histogram and the random GIN never exceed a rejection rate of 0.075 for m ≤ 64 m\leq 64 , whereas degree-corrected signed triangles reach power 0.83 with m = 4 m=4 on D&D and signed 4 4 -cycles need m ∗ = 5.7 m^{\ast}=5.7 on ENZYMES. We chose their normalization in a pilot on D&D ( Section B.6 ).

sections.heading: Calibration with few graphs.
sections.text: With one to three graphs per group ( Table 1 in Section B.3 ), whole-graph permutation never rejects, the Welch normal approximation reaches size 0.21 0.21 at m = 2 m=2 , and only the vertex-split test ( Proposition 2 ) has a finite-sample guarantee at m = 1 m=1 . Conservative variance estimates keep power for first-order visible differences (SBM2 null). Under the Erdős–Rényi null, where the difference is third-order visible, the best method valid for all three nulls reaches power 0.15 0.15 , so with few graphs only first-order differences appear testable without strong assumptions.

sections.heading: 8 Related work
sections.text: With aligned vertices, minimax rates for two-sample testing of inhomogeneous random graphs are known ( Ghoshdastidar et al., 2020 ; Chatterjee et al., 2023 ) . Without alignment, tests compare network statistics of one graph per group ( Ghoshdastidar et al., 2017 ) , latent positions ( Tang et al., 2017 ) , subgraph counts and cumulants ( Maugis et al., 2020 ; Bravo-Hermsdorff et al., 2023 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) , or estimated block models and graphons ( Nguen et al., 2025 ; Sabanayagam et al., 2021 ; Qi et al., 2024 ) , and our excess triangle statistic is the T 3 T_{3} of Gao and Lafferty (2017) . Subgraph counts are the classical moments of network models ( Bickel et al., 2011 ) , and populations of unlabeled networks have been studied through graph distances ( Kolaczyk et al., 2020 ; Lunagómez et al., 2021 ) . Misalignment has been studied for aligned tests with shuffled labels ( Saxena and Lyzinski, 2025 ) and for changepoints ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . The choice of cycle order for one graph is studied for signed polygons, latent geometry and planted subgraphs ( Jin et al., 2021 ; Bubeck et al., 2016 ; Bangachev and Bresler, 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) , and low-degree analyses of invariant tests treat one graph ( Kunisky et al., 2024 ; Carpentier et al., 2025 ; Rush et al., 2026 ; Skeja et al., 2026 ) , whereas our lower bounds are information-theoretic and use independence across graphs. Appendix C discusses more work.

sections.heading: 9 Discussion and limitations
sections.text: Our results suggest that the number of unaligned graphs needed is set by the lowest order at which the difference is visible to invariant statistics. A motif test attains the aligned order of sample size for differences visible at first order, whereas degree-preserving differences from a constant null, first visible through cycles, cost a power of the signal-to-noise ratio and are invisible to tree statistics.

sections.heading: A recommendation for evaluation pipelines.
sections.text: Metrics built from degrees or message passing should be complemented by cycle statistics. A cheap choice is the signed triangle and 4 4 -cycle counts of B = A − d ​ d ⊤ / ( 2 ​ | E | ) B=A-dd^{\top}/(2|E|) , the degree-corrected centring of Jin et al. (2021) , divided by the number of 2 2 -paths, which depends only on the degrees. They need one matrix product per graph, and permuting whole graphs makes the test exact. In our experiments they detected every degree-preserving difference under irregular nulls and the unrestricted rewiring of the protein graphs ( Sections B.5 and B.6 ).

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The sharp rates of Section 3 are for an Erdős–Rényi null and two explicit alternatives. For non-constant nulls we prove upper bounds only, since matching lower bounds would need a second-moment method for nulls that are mixtures over latent positions, which we leave open. Theorem 2 needs a regular null, and part (ii) covers finitely many tree statistics in the dense regime, so message-passing architectures at finite n n remain open. Partially aligned samples, such as networks registered to a common atlas, and tests that first estimate the partition of each graph when t > 1 t>1 are outside our analysis. Apart from the protein graphs, whose alternative is a synthetic rewiring, our experiments are simulations, and the exact small- m m test gives up motifs that cross blocks.

sections.heading: Broader impact.
sections.text: This methodological work mainly bears on the evaluation of generative models of networks, where metrics that ignore cycles can report a good fit for a model that is wrong in ways they cannot detect. We do not foresee negative societal consequences.

sections.heading: A.7 What is not proved
sections.text: • Sharp constants. Theorem 1 (iv) holds with explicit but loose constants. The sharp aligned threshold m ​ t = 1 mt=1 is cited from Chatterjee et al. [2022] (sparse regime) and not reproved, and in the dense regime we only prove 0.87 / t ≲ m al ∗ ≲ C / t 0.87/t\lesssim m^{*}_{\mathrm{al}}\lesssim C/t . The asymptotically sharp unaligned constant (Remark 6 ) relies on the likelihood-ratio limit of Banerjee [2018] . • General finite-rank differences. Only the rank-one and the specific rank-two model are treated. The formula log ⁡ ( 1 + χ 1 2 ) ≈ ∑ j ≥ 3 ( ∑ i ν i j ) 2 / ( 2 ​ j ) \log(1+\chi^{2}_{1})\approx\sum_{j\geq 3}(\sum_{i}\nu_{i}^{j})^{2}/(2j) for a general zero-degree finite-rank H H with normalized eigenvalues ν i \nu_{i} is consistent with both cases but is not proved. The Veblen argument needs the positivity of the coefficients t S t_{S} , which fails in general. • Sparse graphs. Theorem 1 (i)–(iii) and Proposition 1 (i)–(iii) are non-asymptotic and hold for all p p . The distributional statements (Theorem 2 (ii), Proposition 1 (iv) central limit part) are proved for fixed p p only. • Beyond fixed families of signed tree counts. The distributional statement for unsigned tree counts, for degree and colour-refinement histograms with growing support, and for message-passing embeddings at finite n n remains a conjecture (Remark 10 ). Only the graphon-level statement (Remark 8 (c)) follows from Theorem 2 (i) and the cited characterization. • Non-constant nulls. There is no lower bound for non-constant W W , aligned or unaligned. For differences that are visible at first order we prove upper bounds of the same order 1 / t H 1/t_{H} for unaligned and aligned tests (Theorem 3 (iv) and Proposition 4 ). For degree-preserving differences orthogonal to a null of finite rank, the t − 3 t^{-3} rate is a conjecture (Remark 14 ). The improved n − 2 n^{-2} variance for F F -regular nulls is cited. • Power of the vertex-split test. Proposition 2 proves validity and computes the signal-to-noise ratio of the within-block statistic. We do not analyse the power of the permutation test itself at small m m .

sections.heading: B.1 Common settings
sections.text: All experiments ran with NumPy and SciPy on one laptop CPU (10 cores, 16 GB memory), with four worker processes for E11–E14, seven for E15 and three for E16. All data are simulated, except the protein graphs of E16. Wall-clock times were about 24 24 minutes for E11 and E11b together (E11b reuses the graph pools of E11), 11 11 minutes for E12 at n = 128 n=128 and 66 66 minutes at n = 256 n=256 , and 19 19 minutes for the sparse panel. E13, E14 and E14b took 2 2 , 5 5 and 2.5 2.5 minutes, E15 took 14 14 minutes and E16 took 8 8 minutes. The numerical checks of the proofs take about 2 2 minutes in total. Seeds are fixed and recorded with the results. For every reported rejection rate r ^ \hat{r} based on R R replicates, the Monte Carlo standard error is ( r ^ ​ ( 1 − r ^ ) / R ) 1 / 2 (\hat{r}(1-\hat{r})/R)^{1/2} , which is at most 0.016 0.016 for R = 1000 R=1000 and 0.035 0.035 for R = 200 R=200 . The sample size m ∗ m^{\ast} is the smallest m m at which the power reaches 0.5 0.5 . It is obtained by log-linear interpolation of the running maximum of the power curve on the grid of m m values, and is reported as > m max >m_{\max} when the power never reaches 0.5 0.5 on the grid.

sections.heading: Two caveats about CDB.
sections.text: First, K3R \mathrm{K3R} lies outside the theory of Chatterjee et al. [2026] under an Erdős–Rényi null. Second, at n ≤ 128 n\leq 128 the regularity test never flagged a graph as irregular, even under the irregular SMOOTH null. The bootstrap applied to t ⁡ ( K 3 ) t(K_{3}) alone is then anti-conservative under SMOOTH (size 0.18 0.18 – 0.36 0.36 ). With the correct regime its size is 0.023 0.023 – 0.039 0.039 . sections.text: • Degree histogram (degrees 0 0 – 60 60 ). • Local clustering histogram ( 50 50 bins). • Counts of edges, 2 2 -paths, triangles, 3 3 -stars, 3 3 -paths and 4 4 -cycles, each divided by its expectation under 𝔾 ⁡ ( n , p ^ ) \mathbb{G}(n,\hat{p}) . • Normalized-Laplacian eigenvalue histogram ( 100 100 bins on [ 0 , 2 ] [0,2] ). • A random GIN [ Xu et al., 2019 ] with three layers of width 32 32 , constant input and sum readout of all layers. sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: The TUDataset collection [ Morris et al., 2020 ] provides the D&D protein structures [ Dobson and Doig, 2003 ] , in which two amino acids are joined when they are less than 6 6 Å apart, and the ENZYMES tertiary structures [ Borgwardt et al., 2005 ] . As in the Proteins benchmark of graph generative models [ You et al., 2018 , Liao et al., 2019 ] we keep the 918 D&D graphs with 100 100 to 500 500 vertices, and as in Jo et al. [2022] the 587 ENZYMES graphs with 10 10 to 125 125 vertices after removing isolated vertices. The graphs of a dataset differ in size and shape, and both groups are drawn from the same dataset.

sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: Each replicate draws 2 ​ m 2m distinct graphs at random. The first m m form group 1, and the other m m form group 2 after 5 % 5\% of their edges have been rewired by successful degree-preserving double-edge swaps. The three kinds of swaps differ in the pairs of edges they allow. Unrestricted swaps (deg) pick any two edges. Swaps of type wl1 pick two edges whose endpoints have equal degrees, and they preserve the colour of every vertex after two rounds of colour refinement. Swaps of type wl2 pick two edges whose endpoints have equal colours after two rounds, and they preserve the colours after three rounds. Sequences of such swaps preserve these colours, so under wl2 the three-layer GIN returns exactly the embedding of the original graph, which we checked for every rewired graph. Without rewiring the 2 ​ m 2m graphs are exchangeable and all tests are exact. In 1200 replicates at m ∈ { 8 , 64 } m\in\{8,64\} their sizes lie between 0.037 and 0.063. The descriptors are those of E14, adapted to graphs of different sizes. We add a GIN with mean readout, and centre the first signed triangle statistic at each graph’s own edge density. With m = 2 m=2 no two-sided permutation test can reject at level 0.05 0.05 , since the smallest attainable p p -value is 1 / 3 1/3 , so we report m ≥ 4 m\geq 4 .

The signed cycle statistics detect the rewiring with a few graphs. Triangles are the most sensitive on D&D, whose contact graphs are highly clustered, and 4 4 -cycles on ENZYMES. The clustering histogram and the spectrum also detect it on D&D, but need more graphs on ENZYMES. On D&D the z z -scores of the same signed counts, which grow with the size of the graph, are much weaker, with power 0.28 against 1.00 at m = 8 m=8 for triangles, while on ENZYMES the two normalizations perform alike. We chose the normalization per wedge after comparing the two on rewired D&D graphs in a pilot, which also fixed the rewiring fraction among { 2 , 5 , 25 } % \{2,5,25\}\% , so the D&D results favour it by construction. Under wl2 only 4% and 6% of the triangles are removed, because two rounds of colour refinement nearly identify the vertices of these graphs. The degree histogram and the random GINs then stay at the level, with rejection rates of at most 0.080, and the signed triangles reach power 0.50 at m = 64 m=64 on D&D. sections.heading: Two-sample testing for graphs.
sections.text: With aligned vertices, minimax rates are known for two-sample testing of inhomogeneous random graphs [ Ghoshdastidar et al., 2020 , Chatterjee et al., 2023 ] . Without alignment, the existing tests compare different kinds of summaries: • network statistics of one graph per group [ Ghoshdastidar et al., 2017 ] ; • latent positions of random dot product graphs [ Tang et al., 2017 ] ; • average subgraph counts, with n n fixed and m → ∞ m\to\infty [ Maugis et al., 2020 ] ; • graph cumulants, which remove lower-order effects and improve power at small sample sizes [ Bravo-Hermsdorff et al., 2023 ] ; • Edgeworth-corrected motif statistics for two networks [ Shao et al., 2026 ] ; • block-model and graphon estimates [ Nguen et al., 2025 , Sabanayagam et al., 2021 , Chen et al., 2019 ] ; • joint laws of subsampled moments [ Qi et al., 2024 ] . Ghoshdastidar et al. [2017] prove minimax optimality for tests built on a given statistic, with a single graph per group. Our lower bounds cover all tests and any number of graphs. Their hard instance (Theorem 10 of Ghoshdastidar et al. [2017] ) is essentially our alternative. It compares the Erdős–Rényi graph with a uniform mixture of two-block models over exactly balanced labellings, with edge probabilities p + γ p+\gamma within and p − γ p-\gamma between the blocks, which is the planted partition ( 1 ) with δ = γ \delta=\gamma up to the balancing of the labels. They show that the total variation distance between the two models tends to zero when γ = o ⁡ ( ( p ⁡ ( 1 − p ) / n ) 1 / 2 ) \gamma=o((p(1-p)/n)^{1/2}) , that is, when t → 0 t\to 0 , so that no test with one graph per group has a small total error. Theorem 1 (i) makes this quantitative for m m graphs per group, since for every graph size and every t < 1 t<1 a test with errors ( α , β ) (\alpha,\beta) needs m ≥ 6 ​ ( 1 − t ) ​ c α ​ β / t 3 m\geq 6(1-t)\,c_{\alpha\beta}/t^{3} graphs, and signed triangles attain this order ( Theorem 1 (ii)). The excess triangle statistic in our experiments is the T 3 T_{3} statistic of Gao and Lafferty [2017] . We use existing statistics and characterize when they are optimal and what they cost. The effect of shuffled labels on the power of aligned tests is studied by Saxena and Lyzinski [2025] . Chen et al. [2026] observe that misalignment hurts changepoint localization when the change lies in the joint law of the latent positions, and is nearly harmless when it lies in their marginal law. This is close in spirit to our distinction between orders of visibility.

sections.heading: Detection thresholds and small subgraphs.
sections.text: Contiguity of block models and Erdős–Rényi graphs below the Kesten–Stigum threshold, and the role of cycle counts, are due to Mossel et al. [2015] , Banerjee [2018] and Banerjee and Ma [2017] , building on small subgraph conditioning [ Janson, 1995 ] . The multilayer, aligned analogue is treated by Chatterjee et al. [2022] . Other one-graph problems where the choice of cycle order matters include: • signed polygons for degree-corrected models [ Jin et al., 2021 ] ; • latent geometry, where signed triangles can be optimal [ Bubeck et al., 2016 ] or suboptimal compared with 4 4 -cycles [ Bangachev and Bresler, 2024 ] ; • planted subgraphs [ Yu et al., 2025 , Elimelech and Huleihel, 2025 ] . Correlation detection between unlabeled graphs [ Wu et al., 2023 , Mao et al., 2024 , Ding et al., 2025 , Ameen and Hajek, 2025 ] asks whether two graphs share a hidden alignment, which is a different problem from ours.

sections.heading: Invariant polynomials and low-degree methods.
sections.text: Low-degree lower bounds exploit invariance under relabelling, and invariant polynomials are combinations of subgraph counts [ Kunisky et al., 2019 , Kunisky et al., 2024 , Carpentier et al., 2025 ] . Testing between two structured models has recently been studied in this framework for one graph [ Rush et al., 2026 , Skeja et al., 2026 ] . Our lower bounds are information-theoretic and exploit independence across graphs.

sections.heading: Fluctuations of subgraph counts.
sections.text: The fluctuations of subgraph counts in graphon models are Gaussian at scale n − 1 / 2 n^{-1/2} when the graphon is irregular with respect to the motif. When it is regular, they are of smaller order and possibly non-Gaussian [ Hladký et al., 2021 , Bhattacharya et al., 2023 , Kaur and Röllin, 2021 , Chatterjee et al., 2026 ] . Resampling methods for network moments include Green and Shalizi [2022] , Lin et al. [2020] and Zhang and Xia [2022] .

sections.heading: Learned two-sample tests and graph neural networks.
sections.text: Kernel and learned two-sample tests [ Gretton et al., 2012 , Liu et al., 2020 , Liu et al., 2021 , Kirchler et al., 2020 , Kübler et al., 2022 ] become permutation-invariant graph tests once the features are invariant. The expressive power of message passing on graphons is characterized by tree densities [ Grebík and Rocha, 2022 , Böker, 2023 , Böker et al., 2023 ] . The same features are used to evaluate graph generative models [ You et al., 2018 , O’Bray et al., 2022 , Thompson et al., 2022 , Krimmel et al., 2025 ] .
